headline: Running LLMs on Android: Memory Is the Bottleneck
summary: On-device LLM inference is blocked by mobile memory limits, not compute. Quantization (4-bit/3-bit) and memory-mapped weight loading via MLC LLM and llama.cpp enable 7B models to run in 4GB RAM. This unlocks private, offline AI for Android apps.

slides.title: Why Your Phone Can't Run LLMs (Yet)
slides.subtitle: Memory walls block on-device AI for developers
slides.body: LLMs need gigabytes of RAM, but phones have limited memory. How do we fit a 7B parameter model into 4GB? The answer changes mobile AI.
slides.deep_dive: Large language models typically require 16GB+ VRAM for inference. Mobile devices share unified memory (4-12GB total) between OS, apps, and the model. This forces aggressive quantization (4-bit, 3-bit) and memory-mapped weight loading to avoid OOM kills. The bottleneck isn't compute—it's memory bandwidth and capacity.
slides.key_fact: Memory capacity, not compute, is the primary blocker for on-device LLM inference.
slides.why_it_matters: Enables private, offline, low-latency AI features without cloud dependency.

slides.title: Tools That Shrink LLMs for Android
slides.subtitle: MLC LLM and llama.cpp bring quantization and memory-mapping to mobile
slides.body: These open-source frameworks convert PyTorch/HuggingFace models to run on Android via GPU/NPU. They handle quantization, kernel optimization, and memory management automatically.
slides.deep_dive: MLC LLM uses TVM compiler stack to generate optimized kernels for mobile GPUs (Adreno, Mali) and NPUs. llama.cpp uses GGUF format with mmap() for zero-copy weight loading. Both support 4-bit/3-bit quantization (GPTQ, AWQ, GGML) reducing 7B models to ~4GB. They expose C++/Java/Kotlin APIs for app integration.
slides.key_fact: MLC LLM and llama.cpp are the two leading frameworks for on-device Android LLM deployment.
slides.why_it_matters: Developers can integrate local LLMs into Android apps without cloud APIs.

slides.title: From Model to Mobile App: The Pipeline
slides.subtitle: Quantize → Compile → Package → Run
slides.body: The workflow: 1) Quantize model to 4-bit, 2) Compile to mobile IR (TVM/GGUF), 3) Bundle weights in APK/AAB, 4) Load via mmap at runtime, 5) Execute on GPU/NPU.
slides.deep_dive: Quantization reduces weight precision from FP16 to INT4/INT3 using calibration data, cutting size 4x. TVM (MLC) or GGUF (llama.cpp) compiles operators to mobile GPU/NPU kernels. Weights are stored as memory-mappable files in app assets. At runtime, mmap() maps weights directly into virtual memory—no full RAM copy. Inference streams weight shards from storage to compute units on demand.
slides.key_fact: Memory-mapped loading (mmap) avoids OOM by streaming weights from storage instead of loading entirely into RAM.
slides.why_it_matters: This pipeline makes 7B models runnable on 4GB phones without swapping.

slides.title: On-Device LLM Runtime Architecture
slides.subtitle: App → Runtime → Compiler Kernels → Hardware
slides.body: The app calls a thin JNI layer. The runtime (MLC/llama.cpp) manages memory-mapped weights and dispatches compiled kernels to GPU/NPU drivers.
slides.deep_dive: Android app (Kotlin/Java) → JNI bridge → C++ runtime (MLC LLM TVM runtime or llama.cpp) → Memory-mapped weight store (GGUF/TVM params) → Compiled kernel library (OpenCL/Vulkan/Metal/NPU driver) → GPU/NPU hardware. The runtime handles tokenization, sampling, and KV-cache management entirely in C++ for zero-GC latency.
slides.key_fact: JNI bridge keeps hot path in C++; Kotlin only orchestrates high-level requests.
slides.why_it_matters: Separation of concerns: app handles UI, runtime handles heavy lifting.

slides.title: How Inference Works on Device
slides.subtitle: Prompt → Tokenize → Kernel Launch → Stream Tokens
slides.body: User input tokenized, then each decoding step: 1) Load weight shards via mmap, 2) Run attention/FFN kernels, 3) Sample next token, 4) Repeat until EOS.
slides.deep_dive: Input text → tokenizer (C++ port) → token IDs. For each step: runtime calculates required weight slices, mmap brings them into page cache, kernel library executes attention + FFN on GPU/NPU, logits copied back, sampler picks next token, appended to KV-cache. KV-cache stays in GPU memory. Process repeats until EOS or max tokens. Output tokens detokenized to text.
slides.key_fact: KV-cache resides in GPU memory; weight shards stream from mmap-backed storage per layer.
slides.why_it_matters: Streaming weights from mmap keeps RAM footprint constant regardless of model size.
slides.processing: Tokenize → Loop: mmap weight shard → GPU kernel (attn+FFN) → Sample → Update KV-cache
slides.output: Generated text tokens streamed to UI

slides.title: Avoid These On-Device LLM Pitfalls
slides.subtitle: Quantization loss, thermal throttling, and memory leaks
slides.body: Don't quantize without calibration—accuracy tanks. Don't ignore thermal limits—sustained inference throttles. Don't load full weights into heap—use mmap or OOM.
slides.deep_dive: Common antipatterns: 1) Using 4-bit without calibration data → perplexity spikes. 2) Running long generations without thermal monitoring → CPU/GPU throttles, latency doubles. 3) Loading weights via Bitmap/ByteBuffer into Java heap → immediate OOM. 4) Ignoring KV-cache eviction → memory grows unbounded. Recommended: calibrate with representative data, implement thermal callbacks, use mmap exclusively, cap context length.
slides.key_fact: Uncalibrated 4-bit quantization can degrade quality more than 3-bit calibrated.
slides.why_it_matters: These mistakes turn a working demo into a crashed production app.
items: Quantize without calibration data → quality collapse
Run sustained inference without thermal throttling handling
Load weights into Java heap instead of mmap
Skip NPU/GPU fallback for unsupported ops

slides.title: Run Your First On-Device LLM Today
slides.subtitle: Add MLC LLM or llama.cpp to your Android project
slides.body: Clone MLC LLM Android demo or llama.cpp Android example. Add dependency, place quantized model in assets, call generate().
slides.deep_dive: MLC LLM: add `implementation 'org.mlc:mlc-llm-android:0.x.x'`, put `.so` libs and quantized model (`.params`) in `assets/`, call `MLCEngine.generate()`. llama.cpp: build `libllama.so` with NDK, add GGUF model to `assets/`, use JNI wrapper `LlamaContext.generate()`. Both provide Kotlin samples. Start with a 3B 4-bit model (~2GB) for broad device support.
slides.key_fact: A 3B 4-bit model runs on most 4GB+ phones; 7B needs 6GB+.
slides.why_it_matters: Zero-cloud LLM integration in under an hour.
takeaways: Clone MLC LLM Android demo or llama.cpp Android example repo
Add Gradle dependency and place quantized model in assets/
Call generate() from Kotlin via JNI—first token in <1s on modern phones
